summary: BG2 at Coatue East Meets West: Laffonts walk through their deck arguing AI is a 15%+ of GDP super cycle and productivity could stabilise debt, with Bitcoin sizing, IPO/venture recovery, and headcount efficiency. Practical advice for growth/profit quadrants.

coverage.note: intro, thanks, conference; optimism and AI market cap slides
AI waves, sector leadership rotation, tech share of GDP, Mag 7 vs AI power
CoreWeave pure play; Bitcoin sizing; venture judgment
institutional vs venture risk, mental flexibility, crypto regulation
Bitcoin as alternative, stablecoin Treasuries, Google and ChatGPT
data joining; ChatGPT impact on Google; adoption
ChatGPT momentum; cloud share vs GPU share
hyperscaler count, chips, token drivers, macro intro, 10-year band
expensive markets, tokens trump tariffs, bond risk, productivity and debt
growth outlook, public market flight path, IPO market reopening
Meta rationale, Anthropic revenue growth, why go public, quasi-public
public disclosure, mark-to-market, margin expansion, Microsoft headcount
low growth quadrants, reinvent, back-foot conservatism

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: that's how everybody thinks first of all, so it's never priced in.
claims.claim: Because investors always fear that the current high is the peak, optimism about a major trend is never fully priced in and things tend to work out.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: one of the reasons these trends get bigger, they're built on all the on top of each other.
claims.claim: Tech waves (mainframe, PC, internet, SaaS, AI) stack on one another, so each is larger than the last.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: right now it's about 50% tech
claims.claim: Market leadership has rotated over centuries (finance and real estate, manufacturing, energy, now about 50% tech), and AI power and semicap suppliers should be counted in the tech trend.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: technology when when we got started Thomas was 5% of global GDP today it's 15% of global GDP
claims.claim: Technology rose from 5% to 15% of global GDP over Coatue's life and will exceed 15% in 10 years.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: so the mag 7 has actually underperformed this year but we have AI power.
claims.claim: In 2025 the Mag 7 were roughly flat while AI power, AI software and AI semis rose, a broadening beyond crowded mega-caps.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: being an AI pure play, there's very few in the public market.
claims.claim: CoreWeave offers pure-play AI exposure, which is rare among public companies with legacy businesses.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: So Bitcoin represents you know two out of 500 of the net worth of the world or 400 whatever it moves a little bit.
claims.claim: Bitcoin (about $2T) is about 0.4-0.5% of world net worth of $450-500T (equities 120T, real estate 100-150T, gold 15-20T), so a rise to $4-6T is plausible and institutions cannot ignore it.
claims.indicator: Bitcoin market cap vs world net worth
claims.testable: partly - sizing logic, not a test

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: the institutional investor is wrong and the retail investor right. Sometimes it's the opposite.
claims.claim: Retail and institutional investors are each right at different times (retail meme episodes vs institutional blind spots).

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: And in fact, sometimes you invested in the wrong company, but it is the right trend. And those bad investment cloud your judgment.
claims.claim: Bad past bets (2020-22 crypto venture) can make investors reject the right trend, so judgement must be separated from past losses.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: And yet, you you showed this slide 18 where you said maybe the volatility of Bitcoin is is coming down which might put it more into an institutional asset class.
claims.claim: Falling Bitcoin volatility may move it into an institutional asset class.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: the appetite for institutions in the public market for assets that are perceived to have significant downside, i.e. like 70 or 80% that are marked to market I have found is just really low.
claims.claim: Public institutions avoid marked-to-market assets with 70-80% downside, whereas private portfolios hold many unmarked bets where a few winners pay for zeros.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: they're proven right at a moment in time because it'll have a 50% draw down and so rather than re-evaluating their priors they lock in to that position
claims.claim: Investors who call crypto a fad get confirmed by 50% drawdowns and then lock in the view instead of updating; mental flexibility is a key investor trait.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: I've made 120% of my money on obvious ideas and I've lost 20% elsewhere.
claims.claim: Druckenmiller: nearly all profit comes from obvious ideas; losses come from the non-obvious, so force yourself to take obvious conclusions seriously.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: The government's gone from being kind of antagonistic towards supportive. That's a big shift because regulatory risk was a big question for all this stuff.
claims.claim: Crypto regulation turned from antagonistic to supportive (stablecoin legislation passed June 2025) and stablecoins have real corporate workflow utility, a reason to re-evaluate crypto.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: Well, what if actually the alternative is Bitcoin, right?
claims.claim: If investors need an alternative to the dollar amid government overspending, Bitcoin could become one.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: when you have a stable coin with interest, how long is it before the government creates a one-year stable coin, a 5year, 10 year, a 30-year stable coin
claims.claim: Interest-paying stablecoins could let the Treasury sell bonds directly to consumers worldwide, bypassing dealers.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: listen, maybe search is under threat, but YouTube is with all this new AI content going to explode and potentially threaten Netflix and maybe Whimo is going to also do incredibly well.
claims.claim: Google may lose search share to ChatGPT but has offsetting assets (YouTube, Waymo, Android, Gmail).

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: data is useless unless you can join data sets that don't speak to each other. That is the unlock.
claims.claim: Joining alternative data sets (100M credit card receipts per day plus email receipts) is where the value arises.
claims.indicator: credit card and email receipt data

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: once he started paying the 20 bucks a month to OpenAI what happens to the usage and you can see peak to trough it's down 8% year-over-year.
claims.claim: Users who subscribe to ChatGPT cut Google page views by about 8-11% (peak to trough, over two years), versus 4% annual growth without it.
claims.indicator: Google page views of ChatGPT subscribers

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: these major shifts, they just start one little step at a time and that one little step becomes a gigantic move quickly.
claims.claim: Small initial shifts in usage can scale quickly into gigantic moves, so do not underestimate them.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: the fact of the matter is Chat GPT has been radically more resilient and the engagement has increased much faster than I think any of us would have thought
claims.claim: ChatGPT's adoption beat Twitter, Instagram, Facebook and TikTok and held up despite new entrants (Gemini, Grok, Meta), with no virality.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: we're starting to see network effects right on the data side. We're starting to see switching costs with permanent memory
claims.claim: Network effects and switching costs from permanent memory begin to protect ChatGPT.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: Amazon notably 44% of cloud revenue market share but only 20% of Nvidia GPU allocation and then Oracle jumps from 5 to 19 and Core comes out of nowhere to be 11.
claims.claim: Share of Nvidia GPU allocation differs from cloud revenue share: Amazon 44% vs 20%, Oracle 5% vs 19%, CoreWeave 11%, Microsoft and Google matched at 30/20.
claims.indicator: cloud revenue share vs Nvidia GPU share

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: either AWS is behind in AI, that could be one, or they're pursuing a different hardware strategy
claims.claim: Amazon's low GPU share means AWS is behind in AI, is using its own chips, or Nvidia avoids a dominant customer.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: are Nvidia GPUs a prediction of future cloud revenues
claims.claim: Key question: whether GPU allocation share predicts future cloud revenue share (estimates +/-5-6% noisy).
claims.testable: yes - test GPU share vs later cloud revenue

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: like a dozen hyperscalers than like the two or three that we the overseas sovereign
claims.claim: With Stargate, Anthropic, sovereigns and telecoms, there could be a dozen hyperscalers instead of two or three.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: In the internet era, almost every startup started with Oracle and Sun and 5 years later they weren't on it.
claims.claim: There is precedent for infrastructure standards shifting: some AI players will stay on Nvidia while others build custom chips (Google TPU, Amazon).

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: and maybe a super cheap model just for some very local application. maybe that could run on a custom chip.
claims.claim: Expensive reasoning models may run on Nvidia while cheap local models run on custom chips.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: So what's really driving inference and and this token explosion like consumers first and foremost
claims.claim: Token growth is driven by consumer applications, so cloud providers backing ChatGPT (Microsoft, Oracle, CoreWeave) need more GPUs than Amazon.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: We've been in a band between 35 and basically 48 now for two years.
claims.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield has stayed in a 3.5-4.8% band for two years despite 'debt spiral' calls of 6.5-7%.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: If you don't do macro, macro does you.
claims.claim: Macro matters even for fundamental investors but obsessing about it can undo you.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: markets were expensive the '9s during the PC and internet era and the market did well.
claims.claim: Expensive markets (as in the 1990s) can keep doing well, so valuation alone is not a reason to exit.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: this doesn't feel to us like I like to say that the tokens trump tariffs right basically
claims.claim: AI productivity matters more than tariffs for the equity outlook, though tariffs may not have passed through inflation yet.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: A 30-year bond at 4 and 1.5% on its way to 6 or 7, you could lose 60 or 70% of your money.
claims.claim: Long-bond buyers at 4.5% risk large losses if yields rise, so it is puzzling they buy unless productivity makes lower rates plausible.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: if productivity for the next decade or so was about 2 and a half to three and a half% per year we could achieve substantial reductions in this key ratio of debt to GDP
claims.claim: With 2.5-3.5% productivity growth for a decade, debt/GDP could stay near 80-100% instead of rising to 140%, as in the 1990s PC and internet productivity gains.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: was supposed to go from 40 to uh or 60 to 80 by expert and it in fact went from 60 to 40.
claims.claim: In 1993 experts projected debt/GDP rising to 80% but it fell to 40%, so fiscal forecasts can be badly wrong.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: you would end up with with GDP growth way more in like the 5% plus, maybe even six, which by the way, that was the case for many of the years in the 90s.
claims.claim: A productivity boom could produce nominal GDP growth of 5-6%, as in the 1990s.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: tariffs fairly much being under control multiples are you know pretty full but like they were in the '90s they can stay full
claims.claim: Public flight path: tariffs manageable, multiples full as in the 1990s, 10-year in the fours, plus an AI super cycle.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: the signals are going from red to I would say yellow and potentially green.
claims.claim: After the unhealthy 2021 cycle (too much capital in, record-low IPOs, even worse than post-financial crisis), venture exits are improving.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: the 2021 cohort within one year of going IPO was down 40% and 5 years later is down 50%.
claims.claim: The 2021 IPO class (excluding SPACs) was down 40% after one year and 50% five years on, about 75% down versus the market.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: we have better IPOs that are being rewarded
claims.claim: Strong recent IPOs (CoreWeave, Circle) with clear disclosure and average rule of 40 show public markets rewarding growth plus profitability, and M&A is returning.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: they're paying a $30 billion valuation. So, they're b paying effectively 15 billion. They're avoiding regulatory scrutiny.
claims.claim: Meta's structure to buy 49% of Scale AI at a $30B valuation (about $15B) avoids regulatory scrutiny, showing urgency and the size of the AI prize, at roughly 1% of Meta's market cap.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: it took him about a year to get to their first billion in revenue. It took him three months to get to the next billion and then it took him two months
claims.claim: Anthropic revenue accelerated: about 12 months for the first $1B, 3 months for the next, 2 months for the next, showing AI revenue growth speed.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: I happen to believe that all these companies should go public.
claims.claim: Large venture-backed firms should list for financing, discipline, brand and retail participation (democratization).

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: These are companies over five or 10 billion dollars in value. They would have all been public 10 or 15 years ago.
claims.claim: A quasi-public tier of companies above $5-10B stay private because private markets, private equity continuation funds, secondaries and private credit now have the depth to fund them.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: if you're not willing to submit yourself to sort of the sunshine and the and the ray of light of the public markets, you're going to get it through a regulatory agency.
claims.claim: Very large private companies get regulated anyway, so staying private does not avoid scrutiny.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: every day we learn something and every day we know it's the it's the price you can get today.
claims.claim: Mark-to-market is imperfect and volatile but informative every day.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I call a game the golden age of margin expansion.
claims.claim: The Mag 7 grew over 20% compounded for 3-4 years while opex grew about 2%, a historically unseen margin expansion driven by AI efficiency.
claims.indicator: Mag 7 revenue growth vs opex growth

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: Chapter one is the zer era. It's co software is everywhere. The only way these companies think they can grow is by hiring more people.
claims.claim: Microsoft headcount shows zero-rate hiring, then a 'get fit' stabilization, and now an AI era where it may have hit peak headcount.

claims.speaker: Philippe Laffont
claims.quote: doubles the size of the company as the employee count is down over 35%.
claims.claim: AppLovin doubled revenue per employee in four years, revenue doubled while headcount fell 35% as it right-sized and used AI.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: Google has 187,000 employees. Open AAI 2700.
claims.claim: Google has 187,000 employees against OpenAI's 2,700, showing small lean AI-native firms can take share.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I'm going to 3x the company and our headcount may not grow or only grow a little bit.
claims.claim: Jensen Huang plans to triple Nvidia with flat headcount because agents will report to him.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: there's a level of confidence in a company's use of AI if they're willing to actually reduce headcount.
claims.claim: A willingness to cut headcount is a credible signal of genuine AI use, versus lip service.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: If a lot of companies are doing this and you you pile them all together, right, you're going to get more output for a fixed amount of labor and capital
claims.claim: Firm-level AI efficiency aggregates into economy-wide productivity.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: it's possible that companies need less employment but more companies get created because it's much easier to create a company.
claims.claim: AI may cut labor per company but increase firm formation (Jevons-type effect), so unemployment may fall rather than rise.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: So our advice being to entrepreneurs that if you are growing over 25% you are profitable time to think about whether you should be public.
claims.claim: Coatue matrix: companies growing over 25% and profitable should prepare for an IPO.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: So we have seen in the public market now growth be re-rewarded post 2021.
claims.claim: Public market revenue multiples reward growth and penalize slow growth after 2021, a gap that has widened.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: If you're burning then now might be the time to build a fortress balance sheet.
claims.claim: Growing companies that burn cash should raise large war chests now (OpenAI raised $40B).

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: we have a generational architecture shift time to kind of see how we can play offense.
claims.claim: Profitable low-growth companies should use AI-driven architecture shift to invest and play offense, even accepting losses.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: Everybody said get to cash flow break even. They all ran that way, but that meant cutting headcount, cutting programs that they might have been doing.
claims.claim: After the 2021 correction, companies cut to reach breakeven and ended up in low-growth situations.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: the best word I could come up with is it's time to reinvent and reinvent could mean a lot of different things.
claims.claim: Companies growing under 25% and burning cash should reinvent: go all in on a small fast-growing product or open source an asset.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: they don't internalize the fact that if they stay low growth at this size, their multiple could go from five to three to one, right, times revenue.
claims.claim: Conservative low-growth mid-size companies protect something that does not exist because their revenue multiple compresses toward 1x.

claims.speaker: Thomas Laffont
claims.quote: but I also think there's a lot of benefits to what I'll call more mercenary thinking right which is more reinventing from the ground up right
claims.claim: Combining tribal venture loyalty with public-market mercenary thinking in boardrooms can yield better outcomes.
